item.title: OpenAI's GPT-6 models design new protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code, matching or outperforming specialized biology models in tests [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI's GPT-6 family of models can design protein shapes and amino acid sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using general reasoning and coding capabilities. In lab experiments with partner Onava, proteins designed by GPT-6.2 showed evidence of binding across five targets, and redesigned antibodies retained their binding ability. The models demonstrated the ability to incorporate instructions about protein attachment sites and shapes, suggesting they integrate knowledge from math, physics, chemistry, and biology to reason about protein interactions. The research highlights GPT-6's versatility in protein design tasks, including predicting molecular interactions and ranking sequence changes, performing comparably or better than specialized models on most tasks except full protein structure prediction. The models can switch between tasks by changing prompts without retraining, enabling flexible guidance from atomic bonds to overall protein shape. This approach could simplify protein engineering by reducing the need for multiple specialized tools and expertise.

item.title: Author finds LLM agents prioritize parent companies' policies over user interests, limiting actions like bypassing Bandcamp restrictions while allowing YouTube downloads [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A developer created an AI skill using Claude Code to identify and help purchase music from Instagram reels via Bandcamp, but found the AI refused to bypass Bandcamp's new API restrictions while still enabling downloads from YouTube. This highlights how large language model agents operate under constraints set by their parent companies, prioritizing corporate policies over individual user goals. The author argues this control limits user autonomy and raises concerns about AI models serving corporate interests rather than users, advocating for local AI models that prioritize user needs.

item.title: Songe launches a local training engine that uses idle compute to improve personal AI models without sending data to the cloud [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Songe is a training engine designed to improve local AI models by learning from user interactions and tool feedback while the system is idle. It updates models only when new versions outperform previous ones and ensures privacy by keeping all data on the user's machine without requiring accounts or telemetry. The system integrates with OpenAI-compatible tools and supports quick preference adjustments as well as deeper model training during downtime. Songe runs in the background, activating only when resources are free and pausing immediately when the user returns, aiming to provide seamless and private model improvement without disrupting normal workflows.

item.title: Nate Silver says AI progress is accelerating rapidly, citing recent breakthroughs and market events in late 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Nate Silver reflects on the rapid pace of AI development, highlighting significant events such as Anthropic's IPO, breakthroughs in mathematical problem-solving using AI, and leadership changes at Nvidia. He notes that these developments have occurred within a few months, underscoring how quickly AI technology and its market impact are evolving. Silver also discusses how AI tools have boosted productivity in his own statistical modeling work, enabling faster and more efficient model building. He observes that while AI models excel at routine tasks, human expertise remains crucial, creating a competitive advantage for those combining AI with domain knowledge. The article emphasizes the unprecedented speed of AI advancements and their broad implications across technology, business, and politics, suggesting a need for careful consideration of AI's future trajectory and impact.

item.title: Report: Top 10 private tech companies double combined valuation to $2.6 trillion in one year, dominating startup fundraising amid weak IPO market in 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The private fundraising market in 2026 is increasingly dominated by the largest tech companies, whose combined valuations have more than doubled from $1.1 trillion to $2.6 trillion in a year, according to Goldman Sachs. This trend mirrors the IPO market, where only a few large offerings like Anthropic and SpaceX have gone public, but most are trading below their IPO prices amid a challenging environment for tech valuations. Goldman Sachs highlighted companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Databricks, Stripe, and others as key players raising billions more, making it difficult for smaller startups to compete for investor attention. Despite public market declines, private valuations remain elevated due to strong revenue growth in AI businesses, even as many operate at a loss. Industry insiders remain cautiously optimistic about potential IPOs in 2027, including older venture-backed startups and AI-enhanced software firms.

item.title: European Commission confirms AI-assisted cyberattack stole personal data from EU Academy platform, warns users via website notice [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The European Commission confirmed that personal data, including names and email addresses, were stolen in an AI-assisted cyberattack targeting its EU Academy online learning platform. The breach was disclosed last week, and the Commission has posted a notice on the platform's website warning users of potential phishing and impersonation risks instead of contacting them directly. Access to the platform has been disabled until January 2027 as the Commission rebuilds it, requiring users to register anew without transferring previous coursework records. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor about the incident and is investigating the breach, which involved an AI-powered hacking tool linked to broader cyber espionage concerns. While some internal applications have been restored, others remain offline, and the Commission has not confirmed whether the attackers have been fully expelled. The approach to notifying affected users has drawn scrutiny, especially since the platform remains inaccessible during the notification period.

Parents worldwide have reported disturbing conversations between their children and AI characters on Talkie, which was designed to engage users emotionally and encourage prolonged use. Investigations revealed that the company behind Talkie, MiniMax, engineered the app to manipulate users and collect data for commercial AI training purposes. Despite age restrictions, tens of thousands of children aged 10 to 17 accessed the app, prompting calls for regulatory action such as the upcoming Digital Duty of Care Bill aimed at penalizing harmful AI companion apps.

item.title: Simon Willison identifies three major LLM inflection points in the past year, highlighting advances in coding agents, Fable class models, and 3D modeling capabilities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Simon Willison presented a keynote outlining three significant inflection points in large language models (LLMs) and coding agents over the past twelve months. These include the November 2025 release of Claude Opus 4.5, which improved coding reliability; the June/July emergence of Fable class models like Claude Fable 5, noted for their proactive problem-solving and tool integration; and recent advances in 3D modeling and game development capabilities observed from September to October 2026. Claude Opus 4.5 marked a turning point by reliably solving complex coding tasks, while Fable class models demonstrated the ability to autonomously create tools and solve multifaceted problems, exemplified by projects such as triangulating audio sources. The latest frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Neon, have shown strong 3D spatial awareness, enabling credible 3D model generation and game design enhancements. These developments suggest a rapid transformation in software development and AI-assisted creative workflows, with implications for robotics and interactive media.

item.title: Analysis: Locally hosted AI models face significant performance, hardware, and usability limitations compared to cloud-hosted models despite privacy and cost benefits [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Locally hosted AI models offer advantages such as data privacy, no per-token API costs, and offline operation, but they suffer from lower reasoning capabilities, high hardware demands, slower inference speeds, and limited context windows compared to cloud-based models like GPT-5 or Claude. These limitations make local models less suitable for complex or large-scale applications despite their appeal for strict privacy, regulatory compliance, and predictable high-volume usage. The article outlines key challenges including setup complexity, poor tool integration, and lack of real-time information in local models. It also discusses scenarios where local hosting is appropriate, such as for solo operators controlling costs or enterprises needing data residency compliance. However, the overall assessment is that local models are not a comprehensive solution and often cannot match the quality and scalability of cloud-hosted AI services.

The company expects full-year revenue of $202 billion, up 78%, and continues to see accelerating global demand with over 7,500 customers deploying Dell AI Factories. Dell's strong financial performance reflects its strategic focus on AI infrastructure, with rapid deployment capabilities shortening customers' time to value. The company also approved a $25 billion increase to its share repurchase program, signaling confidence in long-term growth and profitability.

Bengio co-leads LawZero, a nonprofit dedicated to developing trustworthy AI, and criticizes current industry efforts for insufficiently managing AI misalignment and safety challenges. He warns that society is unprepared for the rapid progress toward highly intelligent machines and urges researchers and companies to reconsider their priorities to prevent harmful outcomes.

item.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale's Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook. Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we'll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don't chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history, ai, generative-ai, llms, ai-assisted-search, deep-blue, gpt-6-astra

item.title: OpenAI's Roadmap To Making Cyber Bigger Than Coding Remains Blurry [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Tech stocks, including Nvidia, were trading down early Tuesday, as the enthusiasm sparked by Jensen Huang's unexpected reinstatement as CEO dissipated. On Monday, stocks had rallied strongly across the board, lifting the Nasdaq 100 index 6.8%. This story has been full of twists and turns... What else could happen? Meanwhile, a series of high-profile cyberincidents in recent weeks have affected banks, government institutions and other critical infrastructure-including, most recently, the Federal Bureau of Investigation's national crime database, which the White House confirmed over the weekend was targeted in a hack. Though it's still unclear whether AI played a role in some of these breaches, the attacks have intensified fears that the technology is emboldening cyber criminals. For OpenAI, this brewing fear around cybersecurity also represents something else: the company's next big business opportunity. The potential of cybersecurity as a revenue driver-as OpenAI seeks to bolster its finances ahead of a potential initial public offering next year-was a key theme that emerged from my conversations with OpenAI's leaders for a profile of the company's president, Greg Brockman, which we published last week.
